In fact, the Wayback Machine shows their own homepage said "over 25 years of experience" in 2014, 2018, February 2025 AND September 2025, "over 30 years" in 2023, and only jumped to "over 45 years" (plus the new "100+ apartment communities" line) sometime between Sept 2025 and March 2026. The portfolio claim is similarly inflated: The Real Deal reported in June 2024 that Wiseman "lists on its website nearly 70 apartment buildings," which matches the 72 properties in their own RentCafe search today, not "100+."

Reputation is the real strategic issue. Google reviews aggregate to 3.2 stars across 233 reviews; the recurring positive theme is named on-site building managers (fast repairs, personal attention, large 3–4BR floor plans, walkable Westside/Sawtelle locations, grad-student friendly, pet friendly), and the recurring negative theme is the corporate/leasing office — specifically security-deposit refunds (multi-month delays, a disputed $6,000 check with no proof of mailing) and roommate-turnover paperwork, plus uneven maintenance responsiveness building to building. Separately, there is a published California Court of Appeal opinion, Maarten v. Cohanzad (2023) 95 Cal.App.5th 596, in which former tenants allege the Cohanzads/Wiseman Management LLC used Ellis Act withdrawals to evict rent-controlled tenants and then re-listed units on Airbnb before demolishing the buildings; the court reinstated the class allegations. Wiseman denies wrongdoing. The Real Deal has also written that the company "has evicted hundreds of tenants from rent-controlled properties in Los Angeles, according to the Los Angeles Times," and that preservationists have criticized its demolitions. None of this belongs on the website, but it must shape what the site claims — heritage/legacy puffery and "community steward" language are exactly the claims most likely to be fact-checked against public records.
recommendations: Replace "over 45 years" with something verifiable. Best options, in order: (a) "Building and managing Los Angeles apartments since 1985" — the company's own stated founding year, corroborated independently; (b) "A family-built LA company, licensed to build here since 1982" — anchored to the active CSLB license #417744 issued 02/03/1982; (c) drop the number entirely and say "four decades" / "since the 1980s." Get the client to confirm the founding year in writing before it goes live, because their own archived site said "over 25 years" as recently as September 2025.

Replace "over 100+ apartment communities" with the live count from their RentCafe feed, rendered dynamically if possible ("72 communities across the Westside" today). A precise, checkable number reads more credible than an inflated round one, and it self-corrects as the portfolio changes. If they want a bigger number, "1,000+ homes built" is the claim their own Archinect profile makes.

Add Palms to the neighborhood list. Every recent and pipeline project — three buildings on Motor Ave, two on Venice Blvd, including the 490-unit filing across from Metro's Culver City Station — is in Palms, and the current homepage omits it entirely while listing Brentwood and Hollywood. Suggested list: Brentwood, Sawtelle & West LA, Palms, Venice, Culver City-adjacent, Hollywood.

Build the site's trust argument around the on-site manager, because that is what residents actually praise. Every positive review names a person (Limberth, Josh, Yassine, Dianne) and cites speed. Put a real "your on-site manager" element on each property page, name response-time commitments, and make the maintenance-request flow visible. This converts the one genuine strength into the site's spine.

Answer the deposit objection head-on with a dedicated, plain-English page: how deposits are held, the exact California timeline (itemized statement within 21 days of move-out), how roommate turnovers and partial move-outs are handled, who to contact, and an escalation path with a named role. Multi-month deposit delays and roommate-turnover paperwork are the single most repeated complaint across Google, Yelp, and VeryApt — a site that pre-answers it does more for conversion than any hero image.

Lead with the objectively strong product facts rather than heritage claims: rare 3- and 4-bedroom floor plans (their own long-standing differentiator — "renowned for our rare and highly coveted 3 and 4 bedroom floor plans" has been on their site since at least 2014), in-unit washer/dryer in most units, walkable Westside locations, pet-friendly, on-site managers, online payments. These are verifiable, checkable, and are exactly what the grad-student and roommate-household audience on VeryApt says it values.

Feature Motor Tides with verified specs only: 3557 Motor Ave, Los Angeles CA 90034; seven stories; 104 apartments plus three ADUs; 1–4 bedrooms; rooftop deck; fitness center; pet friendly; leasing (833) 521-3999. Describe the location as "Palms, minutes from Culver City" — not "in Culver City." Do not publish a rent range; the only sourced figure ($483–$5,995) spans deed-restricted units and will be wrong within weeks.

Use the development pipeline as proof of investment, sourced to the trade press: 68 units at 3659 Motor (built), 104 at 3557 Motor (Motor Tides, completing 2026), 200 proposed at 3418 Motor, 490 proposed at 9000 Venice, 119 at 11261 Santa Monica Blvd, 77 at 1600 E Venice, 50 at 1808 Lincoln. This is a real, verifiable "we are still building here" story that does not require any heritage claim.

Mention the affordable-housing component factually and without spin — the 3418 Motor project sets aside 22 units for extremely-low-income households and the 9000 Venice filing sets aside 64. These are conditions of the density-bonus/Expo Corridor and TOC incentives they used, so frame them as "X homes in our pipeline are deed-restricted affordable," not as philanthropy.

Fix NAP consistency as part of the launch: the old 11601 Santa Monica Blvd address and (310) 914-5555 number are still the address of record on CSLB, BBB, Archinect, and Birdeye, while the site says 1520 Federal Ave / 310-473-3000. Update or claim those listings (the Birdeye profile is explicitly unclaimed), and consolidate the duplicate Facebook page and duplicate Instagram handle into one each.

Do a human eye-check on the two things I could not verify before any of it reaches copy: the live Yelp star rating (Yelp blocks automated access; the indexed count is 568 reviews and the rating appears to be 3.7), and whether the client wants the 'Wiseman = family name' origin told at all (DRE records show the founder's former name as "Cohen, Issac Wiseman" — a great brand story, but personal, and his call).

Keep the site's claims narrow and product-focused rather than civic. Given the published Maarten v. Cohanzad opinion and the preservation coverage, any "we preserve neighborhoods," "community stewards," "trusted for generations," or "resident-first since 1980" framing invites a search that ends badly. Specific, checkable, present-tense claims about apartments and service are both safer and more persuasive.
donots: Do NOT say "over 45 years," "45+ years," "since 1980," or "nearly half a century." Nothing supports it, and the client's own archived homepage said "over 25 years of experience" as recently as September 7, 2025 — a 20-year jump in about 15 months that is visible to anyone with the Wayback Machine.

Do NOT say "over 100 apartment communities" or "100+." The Real Deal counted "nearly 70" on their own website in June 2024; their RentCafe search lists 72 today; TRD counted "around 30" in 2022; court filings and CBS said 35 buildings in 2019. No source anywhere supports 100+.

Do NOT state a founding year as fact without written client confirmation. 1985 (their own Archinect bio), 1987 (BBB business-start date), 1982 (CSLB license issue date), and 1980 (LinkedIn/ZoomInfo aggregator data) all appear in public sources and they cannot all be right.

Do NOT claim continuous family ownership of a single company "since 19XX." The brand spans at least four distinct legal names — Wiseman Development & Management, Inc. (alt. names Copac Corp / Wiseman Development / Wiseman Residential), Wiseman Management LLC, COBUILD INC, plus Belmond Homes LP and Hayworth Hyde LLC named in litigation. "Family-owned and family-run" is fine; a continuous corporate lineage claim is not.

Do NOT name any executive other than Isaac Cohanzad as founder, and do NOT assign him a current title (CEO, President, Principal) — no public source states one. Do NOT publish Michael or Benjamin Cohanzad's names or titles without client sign-off; their roles are alleged in a lawsuit and inferred from a BBB entry, not confirmed by the company.

Do NOT use any name scraped from ZoomInfo, RocketReach, ContactOut, or similar aggregators (e.g., a "Financial Analyst" or "Regional Property Manager"). Uncorroborated, and publishing a stranger's name and title on a client site is a real risk.

Do NOT imply the company or its principals hold a California real estate license. Every DRE license is EXPIRED: Isaac Cohanzad (salesperson, exp. 2000), Benjamin Cohanzad (salesperson, exp. 2007), Michael Cohanzad (broker, exp. 2010). No DRE record exists for Wiseman Residential, Wiseman Management, or Wiseman Development. No "licensed brokerage," "our licensed agents," or DRE# in the footer.

Do NOT claim membership in AAGLA, CAA, NMHC, IREM, or any trade body, and do NOT claim any award, "Best of" recognition, certification, or designation. Zero evidence for any of them. Also do NOT display a BBB badge or imply accreditation — BBB lists them as NOT accredited and "Not Rated."

Do NOT claim any BBB rating, "A+" or otherwise. The profile literally reads "BBB does not have sufficient information to issue a rating on this business," with 4 complaints closed in the last 3 years.

Do NOT cite a star rating or review count as a selling point without live verification. Google is 3.2 across 233 reviews — not a number to advertise. The Yelp rating could not be verified directly (Yelp blocks automated access), so no "rated X stars by our residents" claims.

Do NOT publish the Motor Tides rent range. The only sourced figure ($483–$5,995/mo, Urbanize, May 2026) mixes market and deed-restricted units and will go stale fast. "Starting at $2,720" and "479–1,248 sq ft" appeared only in search-engine summaries and were not verified.

Do NOT say Motor Tides is "in Culver City." 3557 Motor Ave, 90034 is in the City of Los Angeles (Palms neighborhood), adjacent to Culver City; Urbanize files every story on it under Palms. "Minutes from Culver City" or "on the Culver City border" is accurate.

Do NOT use preservation, stewardship, or legacy framing — "we preserve LA's character," "restoring historic neighborhoods," "caretakers of the community." The Real Deal reports the company has been "taken to task by historic preservation advocates for demolishing architectural gems across Los Angeles," and their development model is explicitly teardown-and-rebuild.

Do NOT use tenant-tenure or displacement-adjacent claims: "residents stay for generations," "we never displace anyone," "rent you can count on," "a home for life." The Real Deal, citing the Los Angeles Times, reports the company "has evicted hundreds of tenants from rent-controlled properties in Los Angeles," and there is a published appellate opinion on Ellis Act / Airbnb class allegations against its principals.

Do NOT reference, rebut, or allude to the Maarten v. Cohanzad litigation on the website in any form — not as a disclaimer, not as a "setting the record straight" page. It is live litigation (class allegations reinstated on remand, outcome unknown) and any public statement is a legal matter for the client's counsel, not website copy.

Do NOT claim the company "owns" every property it markets, or state a unit count as owned inventory. Sources describe a mix of developed, owned, and managed buildings held through multiple entities and a family trust; "develop and manage" is the safe, sourced phrasing (it is also the company's own wording).

Do NOT publish on-site managers' first names from Google reviews (Limberth, Josh, Yassine, Dianne) as staff endorsements. They are real employees praised by residents, but using their names as marketing requires their and the client's permission.

Do NOT repeat unverified aggregator descriptions that showed up in search summaries — "over 25 years of operation," "15 employees," "founded 1980," "most sought-after buyer of residential development properties in Los Angeles." The last one is the company's own 2013-era Archinect puffery and is unprovable superlative marketing.

Do NOT quote social-media follower counts (~290 Facebook, ~174 Instagram) or use social proof modules seeded with them. All were search-index derived and could not be confirmed; the accounts also require login and are split across duplicate handles.

findings.title: Founding: company's own profile says 1985, founded by Isaac W. Cohanzad — not ~1980
findings.detail: Wiseman Residential's Archinect firm profile (admin: "wisemanresidential", i.e., self-authored) states verbatim: "Established in 1985 by Isaac W. Cohanzad, Wiseman Residential is one of Los Angeles' leading residential developers and management companies. To date, Wiseman Residential has built 1000+ residential units, and specializes in 2, 3 and 4 bedroom luxury condominiums and apartments. Each development houses between 10 to 100 units..." The listed contact is 11601 Santa Monica Blvd, Los Angeles 90025, phone 310-914-5555. A preservation blog (RIP Los Angeles, Feb 2020) independently says "Isaac established Wiseman Residential in 1985." 1985 → 41 years as of 2026, not 45+.

findings.title: The "over 45 years" claim is new and contradicts their own prior site copy
findings.detail: Wayback Machine captures of wisemanresidential.com show the claim history: Feb 2014 — "With over 25 years of experience"; Aug 2018 — "With over 25 years of experience"; Nov 2023 — "With over 30 years of experience"; Feb 2025 — "With over 25 years of experience"; Sept 7, 2025 — still "With over 25 years of experience" and NO "100+ communities" claim anywhere on the page. By the Mar 30, 2026 capture the copy reads "Wiseman Residential has proudly served Los Angeles renters for over 45 years" and "over 100+ apartment communities." So the 45-year and 100+ figures both appeared between Sept 2025 and Mar 2026 — a 20-year jump in roughly 15 months. If the new site repeats "45 years," it is trivially falsifiable from the client's own archived pages.

findings.title: Earliest defensible date is 1982 — an active CSLB contractor license held by COBUILD INC, qualified by Isaac Wise Cohanzad
findings.detail: CSLB record retrieved 9/10/2026: License #417744, business name COBUILD INC, 11601 Santa Monica Blvd, Los Angeles CA 90025, business phone (310) 914-5555 — the same address and phone as Wiseman's Archinect and BBB listings. Entity: Corporation. Issue Date 02/03/1982. Reissue Date 09/25/2013. Expire Date 10/31/2027. Status: "This license is current and active." Classification: B – GENERAL BUILDING. Qualifying individual: ISAAC WISE COHANZAD (certified he owns 10%+ of voting stock). Contractor's bond $25,000 with Atlantic Specialty Insurance (eff. 09/01/2026); workers' comp with Insurance Company of the West through 05/12/2027. This is the single best-documented "since" date available: 1982 = 44 years, and it belongs to an affiliated construction entity, not to "Wiseman Residential" by name.

findings.title: Corporate/name history: Wiseman Development & Management, Inc. — alternate names include Copac Corp; BBB start date 6/28/1987
findings.detail: BBB profile (verified twice, consistent both times): Business name "Wiseman Development & Management, Inc."; Alternate Business Names "Copac Corp," "Wiseman Development," "Wiseman Residential"; Date Business Started 6/28/1987; Years in Business 39; Business Management "Mr. Ben Wiseman, Officer" (contact also shown as "Benjamin Wiseman"); address 11601 Santa Monica Blvd., Los Angeles, CA 90025-2907; phones (310) 914-5555, (310) 473-3000, (310) 312-2960; licensing: #417744, Contractors State License Board, exp. 10/31/2027. BBB Rating: "Not Rated" ("BBB does not have sufficient information to issue a rating"); NOT BBB accredited; 4 complaints closed in the last 3 years; 5 customer reviews. Separately, the published appellate opinion names these related entities: Wiseman Management LLC, Belmond Homes, LP, The Cohanzad Family Trust, and Hayworth Hyde LLC. The brand therefore spans at least four distinct legal names; "Wiseman Residential" appears to be the consumer-facing brand rather than a single continuous 45-year-old company.

findings.title: Where the name "Wiseman" comes from — DRE records show Isaac's former name was "Cohen, Issac Wiseman"
findings.detail: California DRE public license lookup (retrieved 9/10/2026): "Cohanzad, Isaac Wise," Salesperson, License 00831807, Mailing 148 N Canyon View Dr, Los Angeles 90049. Salesperson license issued 03/04/1982. Former Name(s): "Cohanzad, Waiz" and "Cohen, Issac Wiseman." This is a genuinely interesting, verifiable origin story for the brand name (the "Wise"/"Wiseman" is a family name, not an invented marketing word) — but it is a personal-identity detail and should only be used if the client confirms and wants it told.

findings.title: No current California real estate (DRE) license — every principal license is EXPIRED, and no company DRE license exists
findings.detail: DRE lookup, 9/10/2026: Isaac Wise Cohanzad — Salesperson 00831807, status EXPIRED (exp. 02/23/2000), no responsible broker, no disciplinary action. Benjamin Cohanzad — Salesperson 01242347, EXPIRED (exp. 03/09/2007), issued 07/14/1998, no disciplinary action. Michael Cohanzad — BROKER 01753522, EXPIRED (exp. 07/23/2010), issued 07/24/2006; affiliated licensed corporation 01525402 "The Condo Agency" with officer license expired 11/17/2018; no disciplinary action. Name searches for "Wiseman Residential," "Wiseman Management," and "Wiseman Development" return zero DRE records. Conclusion: the site must not imply brokerage services, DRE licensure, or "licensed real estate professionals." (Property management of your own buildings does not require a DRE license in California, so this is not a compliance problem — it is only a copy problem.)

findings.title: Leadership: only Isaac Cohanzad (founder) is publicly verifiable; no titles for anyone else
findings.detail: Isaac Cohanzad — VERIFIED as founder: The Real Deal (June 10, 2024) writes "Wiseman founder Isaac Cohanzad paid a total of $12 million in three separate parcel purchases"; Archinect says "Established in 1985 by Isaac W. Cohanzad"; TRD photo credit reads "Wiseman Residential's Isaac Cohanzad." No current title (CEO/President/Principal) is stated anywhere I found. Michael Cohanzad — LIKELY a principal/owner: CBS News (Nov 2019) calls him "one of Wiseman's owners"; the Maarten complaint alleges "Isaac Cohanzad, Benjamin Cohanzad, and Michael Cohanzad control Wiseman"; his LinkedIn headline reads "Wiseman Development and Management." findings.title: Portfolio size: ~70 buildings is the defensible number; "100+ communities" is not supported anywhere
findings.detail: The Real Deal, June 10, 2024: "Wiseman currently lists on its website nearly 70 apartment buildings within its portfolio of developed and managed properties located throughout the Los Angeles market." findings.title: Reputation, quantified: Google 3.2★ / 233 reviews; VeryApt management score 6.8 vs building 7.9
findings.detail: Google reviews aggregated on Birdeye as of 9/10/2026: "Wiseman Residential has a 3.2 star rating with 233 reviews" (all sourced from Google; Birdeye's own count is 0). VeryApt (a grad-student-focused rental review site) shows Wiseman Management with 10 listings, 91 reviews, a 7.9 building rating but only a 6.8 management rating, with the site's auto-summary "What could be better: Can be unresponsive at times." Smaller samples: WYL 3.5 (6 reviews); RateTheLandlord 1.0 (2 reviews); BBB shows 5 customer reviews and 4 complaints closed in 3 years, business Not Rated and not accredited. Yelp shows 568 reviews at yelp.com/biz/wiseman-residential-los-angeles-2 (review count from the indexed page title); the star rating there appears to be 3.7 but Yelp blocks automated access so I could not confirm it directly — verify by eye before citing.

findings.title: The review split is structural: on-site managers are the asset, the corporate office is the liability
findings.detail: Positive reviews are almost always about a specific named on-site person and about speed: "a huge part of that has been because of Limberth... always been quick to help"; "Josh (manager) got us into the best unit in the building... He's been on top of every repair"; VeryApt reviewers (UCLA Law, UCLA Anderson MBA, Loyola Law students) cite proximity to campus, affordability with roommates, dog-friendliness, quiet buildings, easy move-in. Negative reviews are almost always about the corporate/leasing office and specifically about money: a tenant reporting "a four-month delay in receiving my security deposit refund due to the leasing office's refusal to manage tenant transitions properly" and management "completely refused to get involved" in a roommate conflict; another reporting a security-deposit refund check "of over $6,000" with no tracking number, proof of delivery, or delivery photo, and being told "This is how we do business. We're not responsible." Yelp-surfaced themes match: roommate-turnover documents that waive deposit return, deposits tied to incoming roommates, slow maintenance queues at some buildings, package theft. VeryApt's own summary line is "Can be unresponsive at times." The recurring good/bad pattern is consistent across every platform: the buildings and the on-site staff score well; the back office scores badly, and deposits are the #1 flashpoint.

findings.title: Published appellate opinion: Maarten v. Cohanzad (2023) — Ellis Act / Airbnb class allegations reinstated
findings.detail: Maarten v. Cohanzad, No. B308055, Cal. Ct. App., 2d Dist., Div. 3, filed 9/18/2023, CERTIFIED FOR PUBLICATION (95 Cal.App.5th 596), LA Superior Court No. 19STCV00094. Defendants: Isaac Cohanzad, Benjamin Cohanzad, Wiseman Management LLC, Belmond Homes LP, The Cohanzad Family Trust, and Hayworth Hyde LLC. The complaint alleges (these are allegations, not findings) that "Wiseman Management LLC (Wiseman) owns and operates at least 35 apartment buildings in Los Angeles," that "Isaac Cohanzad, Benjamin Cohanzad, and Michael Cohanzad control Wiseman and have created various shell companies," that Wiseman bought rent-controlled buildings, falsely declared permanent removal from the rental market under the Ellis Act to evict tenants, listed the units on Airbnb ("[v]irtually all the Airbnb listings posted by Defendants had a maximum stay of 1,125 nights"; two hosts linked to defendants' properties had "at least 42 Airbnb listings each"), then demolished the buildings and re-rented new apartments "for as much as $5,195 per month." The Court of Appeal reversed the trial court's order sustaining the demurrer to the class allegations and remanded with directions to reinstate them. CBS News reported Wiseman "denies wrongdoing, and says the firm evicted Joanne Maarten for not paying rent, according to legal filings" and that the company did not respond to requests for comment. I found no public record of the case's outcome after remand.

findings.title: Press has also tied the company to mass Ellis Act evictions and to preservation controversies
findings.detail: The Real Deal (Dec 30, 2022): "The company founded by Isaac Cohanzad has been taken to task by historic preservation advocates for demolishing architectural gems across Los Angeles. Also, the company has evicted hundreds of tenants from rent-controlled properties in Los Angeles, according to the Los Angeles Times." (The LA Times original blocks automated access, so I verified the claim only as TRD reports it.) The preservation blog RIP Los Angeles (Feb 21, 2020) catalogues three specific demolitions it attributes to Wiseman — 419 N. Hayworth (a 1936 Normandy Revival garden court, work begun Feb 12, 2015), 1332 N. Formosa Ave (a 1925 storybook, demolished Jan 21, 2017 after Ellis Act evictions), and 7050-60 Hawthorn Ave in Hollywood — and alleges demolition work without permits and over stop-work orders. RIP Los Angeles is an advocacy/preservation source, not a neutral one; the LA Tenants Union publication thetenant.org is cited elsewhere as saying Wiseman evicted "at least 237 rent-controlled tenants" under the Ellis Act, but that page returned 403 and I could not verify the 237 figure directly. Treat both as advocacy claims. The practical point for the rebuild: "heritage," "stewardship," "preserving neighborhoods," and "community" language will be read against this record by anyone who searches.

findings.title: No awards, certifications, or trade-association memberships found anywhere

summary:
The award-winning tier in real estate / architecture / place right now is not won with effects — it is won with **archival structure plus one restrained motion system**. I inspected the live markup, CSS and JS of ~35 sites, including the current Awwwards winners in this category (ERA Residence, SOTM Aug 2026; LIKOVA and Kononenko, SOTD Aug 2026; Seasats, SOTD Sep 8 2026), the canonical many-project indexes (Herzog & de Meuron, David Chipperfield, OMA, 6a), the hotel-collection sites (Aman, Belmond), heritage family real-estate companies structurally identical to Wiseman (Rudin, founded 1925, 32 properties; Durst), place brands (King's Cross, Base31, ROW DTLA, Culdesac) and serious water brands (Finisterre, Feadship, Seasats). Two findings dominate. First, **every site that handles 30–600 places well treats the index as a catalogue raisonné, not a card grid**: a permanent number or year is the primary identity, the list view is typographic and carries hundreds of rows where a thumbnail grid dies at thirty, and the taxonomy is *place*, not attributes. Second, **the serious water brands do not simulate water** — Seasats ships 26 looping MP4s of real ocean and Feadship 27; neither loads a WebGL shader. Restraint is a palette decision, not an effects decision: Seasats' maritime palette is sage and sand (#b7c8be, #d7c5ba, #2b3922), Finisterre's is oat and slate (#e7ddbb, #405174, #010b13). Not one uses cyan.

The implementable stack is settled and free. ERA Residence (Awwwards SOTM) and Eleos (an actual LA developer, Awwwards HM) both run the identical framework-free stack: **GSAP 3.15 + ScrollTrigger + SplitText + CustomEase + Lenis ~1.3**, and GSAP has been 100% free including all former Club plugins since April 2025. Eleos registers a single brand easing curve (`CustomEase.create('eleos','0.625, 0.05, 0, 1')`) and sets it as `gsap.defaults` — one curve governs the whole site, which is the highest-leverage anti-slop move available. ERA's scroll indicator is pure CSS: one JS-set `--progress` custom property driving two complementary `clip-path: rect()` values with a 24px gap, producing a cut that travels down a line — read sideways, that is a tideline, and it needs no library at all. On platform support I verified against the Web Platform Status API today: same-document View Transitions went **Baseline newly on 2025-10-14** (Chrome 111 / Firefox 144 / Safari 18) and are safe; scroll-driven animations are **still Baseline limited** (Chrome 115, Safari 26, **no Firefox**) so they must be `@supports`-gated with a static fallback; `@property`, `color-mix()`, relative colors, masks, `:has()`, subgrid and container queries are all safe. The danger for Wiseman is not technical — it is that 72 street-named buildings default to a filterable card grid, which is exactly the "database dump" the client will read as generic.
recommendations: Acquire or estimate a year for every one of the 72 buildings — year acquired is enough, year built is better — before designing the index. This is the highest-priority content task on the project. Every heritage index pattern I verified (herzogdemeuron.com's project number, davidchipperfield.com's '2022–', oma.com/projects' year headings, 6a.co.uk's Sort by Year, rudin.com/portfolio's '1925 Founded / 32 Properties') is built on a date. Without it the 72 buildings can only be ordered by rent and bedroom count, which is the definition of a listings site.

Give each building a permanent Wiseman number and put it in the URL, exactly as Herzog & de Meuron do (/projects/708-palace-of-congresses/). Ordered by acquisition, 001 through 072, with Motor Tides as the current highest number. The number does three things at once: it makes the newest building visibly part of a 45-year lineage rather than an outlier, it gives the index a left-hand column that is scannable at speed, and it silently asserts that the collection is finite and stewarded.

Ship the index as three peer views behind real URLs — Register (typographic list), Atlas (map), Plates (image grid) — with the Register as the default. Follow oma.com/projects: 591 text rows work on one page, and a thumbnail grid stops working around thirty. The Register row should be number, building name, street, neighbourhood, year — five columns, no card, no border, no 16px radius, no grey box.

Adopt 6a's two-tier structure literally: a 'Selected' set of ten to twelve buildings that carry the brand, at /buildings/selected/<slug>, then 'All 72 Buildings' as a single link to the complete Register. Curation is a decision someone made, and the visitor can feel the difference between a chosen dozen and a filtered result set. This is the cheapest available fix for 'feels like a database'.

Make neighbourhood the spine and prefer sorting over filtering. The dataset already nests cleanly (West Los Angeles 27 › West LA · Sawtelle 26; Beverly Grove 14 › Fairfax · Sunset 6, Pico–Robertson 2, Miracle Mile 1). Group the Register under neighbourhood headings the way OMA groups under years, and offer Sort by Name / Street / Neighbourhood / Year. Reserve filtering for the separate Availabilities view, where hiding things is the actual job.

Split Portfolio from Availabilities at the top of the navigation, as Rudin does with 'Portfolio / All Availabilities / View Map' as three peers. The Portfolio is permanent, dated, photographed and has no prices on it. Availabilities is a utilitarian table with rent, beds, sqft and a phone number. Your CODEX-CONSULT.md already argues for this split; rudin.com/portfolio is the live proof that a 100-year family owner ships it exactly that way.

Build the entire colour system from two hexes plus an alpha ladder, copying ERA Residence's structure: one deep ink (their #17233b — a navy, deliberately not black) and one warm paper (their #f3f3ec), each declared at 0/5/10/30/60/100% alpha, giving twelve values that cover every hairline, divider, scrim and tint on the site. Then allow at most two accents. For Wiseman the ink should come from Pacific dusk and the paper from LA stucco — but derive them from your own photography, not from a palette generator.

Take the coastal palette from sand and slate, never cyan. The verified evidence: Seasats (SOTD Sep 8 2026) runs #b7c8be sage, #d7c5ba warm sand, #4b5746 and #2b3922 — no blue whatsoever on an ocean-robotics site. Finisterre runs #e7ddbb oat, #405174 muted slate, #010b13 deep-sea near-black. Culdesac runs #f7f3f0 paper, #73859f slate, #af5b22 terracotta. A desaturated slate that reads as 4pm marine layer plus a warm oat that reads as stucco will carry 'coastal light' without a single wave.

Shoot or licence real water footage and loop it; do not write a shader. Seasats ships 26 looping <video loop muted autoPlay playsInline> MP4s and Feadship 27, and neither loads Three.js or any WebGL water. Real Santa Monica Bay footage at 4pm, colour-graded to the site palette, in a small number of restrained placements, is more credible and cheaper than a simulation — and it is the one move that cannot be mistaken for AI output.

Carry the Motor Tides idea forward as a horizon line rather than a wave. ERA Residence's scroll indicator is one JS-set `--progress` custom property driving two complementary clips — `clip-path: rect(0% 100% calc(var(--progress) - 24px) 0%)` on the fill and `clip-path: rect(calc(var(--progress) + 24px) 100% 100% 0%)` on the track — so a 24px gap travels down a line as you scroll. Rotate that to horizontal and it is a tideline crossing a photograph or a wordmark: the water metaphor survives, the cartoon does not, and it costs one custom property and no library.

Use the free GSAP 3.15 + ScrollTrigger + SplitText + CustomEase + Lenis 1.3 stack — it is what both ERA (SOTM) and Eleos (LA, HM) actually run, it is framework-free, and every former Club plugin has been free since April 2025. Copy Eleos's wiring exactly: `new Lenis({lerp: 0.1, autoRaf: false})`, then `lenis.on('scroll', ScrollTrigger.update)` and `gsap.ticker.add(t => lenis.raf(t * 1000))`, which avoids the double-RAF jitter most hand-rolled smooth-scroll builds ship with.

Register one brand easing curve and set it as the global default, the way Eleos does with `CustomEase.create('eleos', '0.625, 0.05, 0, 1')` followed by `gsap.defaults({ease: 'eleos'})`. A single shared curve across every reveal, hover, menu and page transition is the highest-leverage anti-slop move available, because 'generic' in motion is precisely the absence of a consistent curve. Pick one with a slow start and a hard settle — it reads as weight, which is what a 45-year-old company should feel like.

Set every reveal to `start: 'top 85%', once: true` with `stagger: {each: 0.06}`, and use GSAP's `clamp()` trigger syntax (`start: 'clamp(top bottom)'`) for anything near the top or bottom of the document. Reveals that re-fire on scroll-back are one of the clearest dated-2022 tells, and clamp() is the fix for elements that never trigger because they sit too close to a document edge.

Use same-document View Transitions for index↔building navigation — Baseline newly since 2025-10-14, Chrome 111 / Firefox 144 / Safari 18, safe to ship. Put `view-transition-name` on the building's photograph and on its number so both morph between the Register row and the building page. Add `@view-transition { navigation: auto }` on top as a pure enhancement for Chrome and Safari; Firefox simply does an ordinary page load.

Gate any scroll-driven CSS animation behind `@supports (animation-timeline: view())` with a fully-styled static fallback. Verified today against api.webstatus.dev: it is Baseline LIMITED — Chrome 115+ and Safari 26+ ship it, Firefox has no implementation at all. Safe modern CSS you should use freely instead: `@property` for interpolatable custom properties, `color-mix()` and relative colors for the alpha ladder, CSS masks for the soft-edge fades, `content-visibility` on the 72-row Register, plus subgrid, container queries and `:has()`.

Choose a display serif with a documented historical lineage and pair it with one neutral grotesque for data — the pattern shared by every heritage site I read font files from (Aman: Lyon Display + Lyon Text + Whitney SSm; Belmond: Sebenta + Gotham SSm; Shutters on the Beach in Santa Monica: Mr Eaves Sans, the Baskerville-revival companion). Set it on warm off-white paper (#f4f4f2, #f3f3ec, #f7f3f0 are the live values), never pure white. The King's Cross precedent is worth naming to the client: Colophon drew the bespoke 'Battlebridge' face from Victorian lettering physically present on the estate — a typeface can be evidence of place.

Write the content as an institutional record, not marketing copy. Kononenko (SOTD Aug 23 2026) names its nav 'Index, Work, About, Contact' and states 'Founded 2011', award categories with years, and publications cited by issue number. Rudin leads with '1925 Founded / 32 Properties'. For Wiseman: the founding year, the count of buildings, the count of neighbourhoods, the year each building entered the portfolio, the street it stands on. Specific, checkable facts are the fastest route away from AI voice — and they are the only thing on the page a competitor cannot copy.

Borrow the museum 'On View' device for leasing status. Cleveland Museum of Art separates 'Show only: On View | Open Access | Highlights' from its descriptive facets, and Aman renders status as a plain lowercase caption on the property line ('Coming soon', 'Opening 2028'). Put 'Now leasing' / 'Waitlist' / 'Fully leased' in small type on the Register row — never as a coloured pill or badge, which is the single most listings-site component in existence.

Add one small, true, LA-specific instrument rather than a decorative flourish — Eleos runs a live 'Los Angeles, CA — 00:00 AM, PST' clock in its header. For a portfolio built on coastal light, a live sun-position or golden-hour indicator, or a marine-layer note, would be defensible, cheap, and impossible to mistake for a template. One such device, not three.

Run the 200px silhouette test on the finished homepage before showing the client: render it at 200px wide in black-on-white beside Douglas Emmett, Kilroy, Essex and two LA competitors. If the Wiseman silhouette is not immediately identifiable, the layout is structurally generic regardless of how good the photography is.
donots: Do not ship the 72 buildings as a filterable card grid. It is the single decision that will make the site read as a database dump, and it is the default that both AI tooling and every mediocre property site converge on. OMA proves a text list carries 591 items; a card grid stops working around thirty.

Do not put a filter sidebar in front of the collection. Filtering hides things and asks the visitor to do inventory work before they have been given any reason to care. Sort a complete list instead (6a: 'Sort by: Name | Location | Type | Year'); reserve filtering for the separate Availabilities view.

Do not use SVG wave dividers between sections, animated gradient wave backgrounds, or any literal wave shape. The client has already rejected this and the category evidence is unanimous: no serious water brand I inspected uses one.

Do not write a WebGL water shader. Seasats (Awwwards SOTD, an ocean-robotics company) and Feadship (superyachts) both ship real looping MP4 footage and load zero shader code. A simulation is more expensive, slower, harder to art-direct, and reads as a tech demo rather than a place.

Do not use saturated cyan, teal, or 'ocean blue' anywhere in the palette. Every credible coastal palette I read from live CSS is desaturated sand plus slate or sage — Seasats #b7c8be/#d7c5ba, Finisterre #e7ddbb/#405174, Culdesac #f7f3f0/#73859f. Cyan is the kitsch tell.
Do not set headlines in Inter, Roboto, or Open Sans, and do not use a purple-to-blue gradient anywhere. These are the two most-cited AI-slop signatures in 2026 and they will be recognised instantly.

Do not draw a grey box with a 16px radius around every item. It is named as the single most reliable slop tell. Separate content with whitespace first, then a 3–5% background-lightness shift, and stop as soon as it reads.

Do not ship the same generic fade-in on every element, reveals that re-fire on scroll-back, hover states that do nothing, or buttons that snap instead of easing. Use one registered brand curve as `gsap.defaults` and `once: true` on every reveal.

Do not ship scroll-driven CSS animations (animation-timeline: view()/scroll()) ungated. Verified today: Baseline limited, and Firefox has no implementation at all. Without an `@supports` guard and a static fallback, Firefox visitors get invisible or broken content.

Do not rely on cross-document view transitions or CSS anchor positioning as load-bearing behaviour — both are Baseline limited with no Firefox support. Same-document view transitions are fine (Baseline since 2025-10-14); cross-document is enhancement only.

Do not put rent prices, bedroom counts, or coloured availability badges into the Portfolio view. Aman, Belmond and Chipperfield all keep the collection view free of transactional data and demote status to a lowercase caption. Rudin makes the split structural, with Portfolio and All Availabilities as separate top-level doors.

Do not let Motor Tides set the visual standard for the other 71 buildings. Your own CODEX-CONSULT.md flags this; the fix is the archive number, which frames the flagship as the most recent entry in a 45-year sequence rather than the implied norm.

Do not animate or headline any portfolio count until it is verified. The current public site says '100+ apartment communities' while the working dataset holds 72 — those describe different things, and a large animated counter on a number that cannot be substantiated is both a credibility risk and, visually, a startup-metrics cliché.

Do not claim any site, award, date, or typeface I have not listed here. Every URL in this report returned HTTP 200 and every font name, hex value, CSS rule and JS configuration was read from the live markup or from api.webstatus.dev on 2026-09-10. Illoca (SOTD Sep 4 2026) in particular is an AI architecture-software product, not an architecture studio — do not cite it as a place site.

Do not use stock photography of people, drone footage of generic coastline, or AI-generated imagery. The buildings are named after their own streets — Brockton, Beloit, Armacost, Penmar, McClellan — and the entrances, courtyards and stucco of those actual addresses are the only imagery that can prove 45 years in Los Angeles.

findings.title: Herzog & de Meuron's project index is the single best model for the 72-building problem — identity is a permanent number, and filters are real URLs
findings.detail: The index at /projects/ offers three peer views — Grid, List, Map — each a genuine URL (?view=list, ?view=map), with Filter and Search as siblings. Every project carries a permanent sequential archive number and the URL bakes it in: /projects/708-palace-of-congresses/, /projects/694-hudson-mosaic/, /projects/498-harvard-graduate-school-of-design-gund-hall-extension/. The List view is purely typographic — number, name, then place on a second line ('708 Palace of Congresses / Tirana, Albania') — and carries the entire back catalogue without images. The filter facets are Type, Year, Status, Location, and each facet is a plain link (?filter=residential&view=list), so the whole system is shareable, crawlable and works without JS. The number is the thing that converts a database into an archive: it asserts that the collection is continuous, dated and finite, and that the newest entry belongs to the same lineage as the oldest. Rendering is Alpine.js over server data, but nothing about the pattern requires it.

findings.title: 6a architects solves 'curated not database' with a two-tier index: a hand-picked Selected set, the full archive behind one link, and sort instead of filter
findings.detail: The landing index shows exactly 17 hand-chosen projects under the heading 'Selected Projects' — Skinners' Hall, Tate Liverpool, Fashion Museum Bath, Cowan Court, Raven Row, South London Gallery, Photography Studio for Juergen Teller — followed by a single link, 'More Projects'. The tiering is encoded in the URL itself: selected projects live at /projects/selected/skinners-hall, not /projects/skinners-hall. Critically, the full index offers 'Sort by: Name | Location | Type | Year' rather than a filter panel. Sorting reorders a complete list and keeps every item visible; filtering hides things and makes the visitor do inventory work. For a 72-item collection this is the cheapest possible fix: a dozen buildings carry the brand, the remaining sixty are one click away and fully sortable, and nobody ever sees an empty filtered state.

findings.title: OMA puts 591 projects on one page and it works — because the list is text, grouped under year headings
findings.detail: The /projects page contains 591 unique project links in a single document. It survives because the default view is a text list grouped under large year headings (2026, 2025, 2024, 2023…), with controls limited to Filter (Status, Typology, Program) and 'View as: List | Map'. There are no thumbnails in the default state and no lazy-loading machinery — no loading="lazy", no content-visibility, no IntersectionObserver in the markup. The lesson is blunt and quantitative: a typographic list scales to hundreds of rows, a thumbnail card grid becomes unreadable somewhere around thirty. If Wiseman's 72 buildings are cards, the page is a spreadsheet; if they are rows grouped by neighbourhood or by year, the page is a register.

findings.title: Chipperfield, Aman and Belmond all use the same collection grammar: geography as the tree, status as a quiet caption, no numbers competing with names
findings.detail: Chipperfield's /projects offers Grid | List | Filter with sort 'Oldest / Newest', facets Typology and Country, and renders each project as name plus an open-ended year ('National Archaeological Museum 2022–'). The open en-dash is doing real work: it says in-progress without a badge. Aman's index is a strict three-level geographic tree — Region › Country › Property — where each property is just name plus place ('Amangiri / Canyon Point, Utah, USA'), and status appears as a plain lowercase caption on the same line ('Coming soon', 'Opening 2028', 'Reopening soon'). No pricing, no ratings, no availability counts anywhere in the collection view. Belmond's /hotels does the same: 'View by: Product | Map', then Region → Country. Across all three, the thing that reads as curation is that the taxonomy is *where*, and every transactional fact has been demoted to a caption or moved off the page entirely.

findings.title: Rudin — a family real-estate company founded 1925 with 32 properties — separates Portfolio from Availabilities at the top level, and owns a single laddered brand colour
findings.detail: This is the closest structural analogue to Wiseman that exists. rudin.com/portfolio leads with 'By The Numbers: 1925 Founded / 32 Properties / 13.1[M sf]'. In the primary navigation, 'Portfolio', 'All Availabilities' and 'View Map' are three peer items — the curated collection and the transactional vacancy list are behind different doors, which is precisely the split your own CODEX-CONSULT.md already argues for. Portfolio sub-facets are asset classes (Office, Residential, Retail, Professional Suites, Development), and the Company section runs 'History & Philosophy / Rudin Values / Leadership / Culture / Philanthropy'. The colour system is one hue in five steps and nothing else: #006e51 primary, #004f3a dark, #b0d0af light, #d7e3d3 and #e9f0e7 tints. A single proprietary colour laddered five ways is what reads as institutional; a palette of unrelated accents is what reads as a template.

findings.title: ERA Residence (Awwwards Site of the Month, Aug 2026) builds its whole palette from two hexes plus an alpha ladder, and its scroll indicator from one CSS custom property
findings.detail: Palette, read from era-residence.webflow.shared.c9555a234.min.css: --base-0 is #f3f3ec (warm bone paper) and --base-1000 is #17233b (deep navy ink, deliberately not black), and each is declared at 0/5/10/30/60/100% alpha — #f3f3ec0d, #f3f3ec1a, #f3f3ec4d, #f3f3ec99, and the same ladder for #17233b. Every hairline, scrim, divider and tint in the site is one of those twelve values. Accents are exactly three and used sparingly: #b5cedb 'powder sky', #f8bbcb 'blush bloom', #340c24 'velvet plum'. Type is Maison Neue Extended for display with sloop-script-three (Adobe Fonts) as a script accent. The scroll-progress mechanic is pure CSS driven by one JS-set variable: [data-s-bar-fill] uses `clip-path: rect(0% 100% calc(var(--progress) - var(--24px)) 0%)` and [data-s-bar-track] uses `clip-path: rect(calc(var(--progress) + var(--24px)) 100% 100% 0%)`, with `--progress: 0%` in the inline style. Two complementary clips on a shared line, separated by a 24px gap, produce a cut that travels downward as you scroll. They also fade scrolling text with `mask-image: linear-gradient(180deg, rgba(255,255,255,0) 0%, #fff 5.29%, #fff 84.62%, rgba(255,255,255,0) 100%)` instead of a hard edge.

findings.title: Eleos — a real Los Angeles developer with an Awwwards Honorable Mention — shows the exact free vanilla stack and the one discipline that separates it from AI output
findings.detail: eleos.la loads gsap 3.15.0 + Observer + CustomEase + ScrollTrigger + DrawSVGPlugin + SplitText, plus lenis 1.3.23 — no framework. The load-bearing details in its inline JS: (1) one brand ease registered globally, `CustomEase.create('eleos', '0.625, 0.05, 0, 1')` then applied via `gsap.defaults({ease: ...})`, so every motion on the site shares one curve; (2) Lenis wired correctly — `new Lenis({lerp: 0.1, autoRaf: false})`, then `lenis.on('scroll', ScrollTrigger.update)` and `gsap.ticker.add(time => lenis.raf(time * 1000))`, which avoids the double-RAF jitter most builds ship with; (3) reveals use `start: 'top 85%', once: true` with `stagger: {each: 0.06, from: 'start'}` — they fire once and never re-animate on scroll-back; (4) the footer parallax scrubs `yPercent: -25` between `start: 'clamp(top bottom)'` and `end: 'clamp(top top)'` — GSAP's clamp() syntax, which stops elements near the document edges from never triggering; (5) hover animations are gated behind `matchMedia('(hover: hover) and (pointer: fine)')` and there is an explicit `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` check. The site also carries a live 'Los Angeles, CA — 00:00 AM, PST' clock in the header: a cheap, non-kitsch assertion of place.

findings.title: GSAP and all former Club plugins have been free since April 2025 — SplitText, DrawSVG, MorphSVG, CustomEase, ScrollTrigger, no key or token
findings.detail: Following Webflow's acquisition, GSAP became 100% free for all users and all commercial projects in April 2025, and Club GSAP is no longer a paid tier. No plugin requires a membership, license key or auth token. This matters because the two award-winning reference builds above (ERA, Eleos) depend on SplitText and CustomEase specifically, and both are now free. It removes the usual argument for hand-rolling a weaker scroll system in a vanilla-JS project — GSAP is framework-free by design and drops into a plain HTML page with two script tags.

findings.title: Platform reality check, queried today: View Transitions are safe, scroll-driven animations are NOT (no Firefox), and the safe modern-CSS set is larger than most builds use
findings.detail: Verified against api.webstatus.dev on 2026-09-10. SAFE NOW: same-document View Transitions — Baseline newly 2025-10-14, Chrome 111 / Firefox 144 / Safari 18. Registered custom properties (@property) — Baseline newly 2024-07-09, Safari 16.4. color-mix() — Baseline widely 2023. Relative colors — Baseline newly 2024-09-16. CSS masks — Baseline widely 2023-12-07. :has() — widely. Subgrid and container queries — widely. content-visibility — Baseline newly 2025-09-15, Safari 26. light-dark() — newly 2024. NOT SAFE: scroll-driven animations (animation-timeline: view()/scroll()) — Baseline LIMITED, Chrome 115+ and Safari 26+ but Firefox has no implementation at all; MDN still flags it 'not Baseline'. Cross-document view transitions (@view-transition { navigation: auto }) — Baseline limited, Chrome 126 / Safari 18.2, no Firefox. Anchor positioning — limited, effectively no shipping support recorded. Practical consequence: scroll-driven CSS animation must sit inside `@supports (animation-timeline: view())` with a fully-styled static fallback, and cross-document view transitions are a pure progressive enhancement that degrades to an ordinary page load.

findings.title: Serious water brands do not simulate water — they shoot it, and they build the palette from sand and slate, never cyan
findings.detail: Seasats (Awwwards SOTD, Sep 8 2026, by Raw Materials) is an ocean-robotics company whose entire site is water. Its markup contains 62 .mp4 references and 26 <video loop muted autoPlay playsInline preload="auto"> elements, and zero WebGL, zero Three.js, zero shader code. Feadship, the Dutch superyacht builder, is identical: 27 .mp4s, five <video> tags, no shader. Both sites are about water and neither renders water. The palettes are the second half of the lesson. Seasats: #b7c8be (sea-glass sage), #d7c5ba (warm sand), #8e9489, #757d70, #4b5746, #2b3922 — a maritime system built from desaturated greens and sand, with no blue at all. Finisterre, the UK cold-water surf company: #e7ddbb (oat, used 83 times), #010b13 (near-black deep-sea), #405174 (muted slate), #676986. Feadship is simply rgb(33,33,33) on white. The kitsch tell is saturated cyan, animated gradient waves, and SVG wave dividers; the credible version is real footage plus a desaturated sand-and-slate ladder.

findings.title: King's Cross is the definitive precedent for heritage place-branding typography: a bespoke face drawn from lettering physically on the site
findings.detail: The King's Cross estate identity, by SomeOne with type foundry Colophon, is built on 'Battlebridge' — a sans drawn from the Victorian lettering visible on the estate's own building facades, including ghost signs and the Coal Office at Granary Square — and named after the district's pre-19th-century name. The live site serves Battlebridge-Bold.woff2 alongside English1766-Semibold.woff2, an 18th-century Caslon-era revival, as the serif companion. The principle transfers exactly: a heritage company's typeface should have a documented lineage tied to its place and period, not be a currently-fashionable grotesque. Related place brands confirm the palette half of this: Culdesac runs GT Pressura + Mabry Pro + P22 Mackinac on #f7f3f0 warm paper with #080808 ink, #73859f slate and #af5b22 terracotta.

findings.title: What established, non-startup brands actually set their type in — verified from live font files, not from memory
findings.detail: Read directly from @font-face declarations and served .woff2/.otf filenames. Aman: Lyon Display Light + Lyon Text Regular (Commercial Type) with Whitney SSm — a Dutch-inflected transitional serif over a workhorse humanist sans; this is the reference luxury-heritage pairing. Belmond: Sebenta (DSType, contemporary serif) + Gotham SSm, on #f4f4f2 paper with a #c04e37 terracotta accent. Proper Hospitality (Los Angeles): GT Sectra Display + GT Sectra Fine + ABC Arizona Mix + Benton Sans Wide + GT Walsheim. Shutters on the Beach (Santa Monica): Mr Eaves Sans — the humanist companion to Mrs Eaves, itself a Baskerville revival — with Gyst Variable, on a pale #e7edf6 blue-grey paper. Snøhetta: Dovre Social Light. David Chipperfield: a bespoke 'GrotesqueDCA'. 6a architects: Nimbus Roman No9 SC, a small-caps roman that reads as archival. Irvine Company: Bodoni + Gotham. Douglas Emmett: Gotham alone — this is the plain LA institutional baseline you are trying to beat. The consistent pattern in the good ones is a serif with a real historical lineage for display, a neutral grotesque for data, and a warm off-white paper (#f4f4f2, #f3f3ec, #f7f3f0) rather than pure white.

findings.title: Museum collection browsers offer two devices worth stealing: a status filter on the object itself, and display-density control
findings.detail: The Cleveland Museum of Art's collection search exposes 'Show only: On View | Open Access | Highlights | Objects in 3-D' as a distinct band above the ordinary facets (Artist Name, Culture, Title, Medium, Location), plus 'Sort By: Relevance' and a 'Display Type: List | Grid' toggle. 'On View' is a status question about the object's current availability to a visitor, deliberately separated from its descriptive metadata — the exact analogue of 'now leasing' versus 'built in 1987 on Brockton Ave'. The V&A's Explore the Collections does the same with 'With image | On display | View by appointment' plus a Dates from/to year range, over 1.25 million objects. Herzog & de Meuron's grid additionally carries a +/- density stepper that changes thumbnail size, letting the visitor choose between browsing and scanning without leaving the page.

findings.title: Current SOTD/SOTM winners in this exact category, with the specific mechanic each is known for
findings.detail: ERA Residence (era-residence.com) — Awwwards Site of the Month, Aug 2026, by The First The Last: a day/night scene switcher and the two-clip --progress scroll line described above; stack is GSAP 3.15 + ScrollTrigger + SplitText + CustomEase + Lenis 1.3.21 + Lottie, fonts from Typekit. LIKOVA (likova.space) — SOTD + Developer Award, Aug 19 2026, by Vide Infra: numbered chapter sections (1 Concept, 2 Location, 3 …) with headline copy repeated in two typographic registers, WebGL present (18 references) but used behind, not instead of, the architecture. Kononenko Architectural Bureau (kononenkogroup.com) — SOTD + Developer Award, Aug 23 2026: navigation is literally 'Index, Work, About, Contact', and the content is written as an institutional record — 'Founded 2011', award counts with categories and years, publications cited with issue numbers ('No. 5 (216) 2024'), offices listed with full street addresses. Seasats (seasats.com) — SOTD Sep 8 2026, by Raw Materials: the real-footage water approach plus per-letter split nav labels. Also verified live and worth studying: 250 Broadway and 360 Lexington Ave (both by übernatural, Awwwards HM), which run PP Editorial New Ultralight + PP Neue York and Instrument Sans respectively; Base31 (base31.ca, Signifly), a place brand that resolves into three sub-brands with their own logos; Storey Architecture (storeyarchitecture.co.uk), whose project index is explicitly labelled 'Hover + click to visit projects'.

findings.title: The 2026 AI-slop signature, stated concretely — and the 200px silhouette test that catches it
findings.detail: The named tells, consolidated from current design-press analysis: Inter or Roboto as the headline face with a system fallback and no second typographic decision; a purple-to-blue gradient in the hero, the CTA and background accents; an oversized centred hero with a vague aspirational headline ('Build the future of', 'Your all-in-one'); three-column card layouts with a uniform 16px border-radius, identical padding and identical card heights; a grey box drawn around every card (named as the single most reliable tell); soft glass panels and oversized rounded corners; abstract 3D blobs and AI illustrations that are slightly too smooth and too symmetrical; stock photography of people at laptops; hover states that do nothing; buttons that snap instead of easing; and the same generic fade-in applied to every element on the page. The diagnostic offered is the lookalike test: reduce the homepage to a 200px-wide black-on-white silhouette and place it beside five competitors — if you cannot identify yours, the page is structurally slop. For this project specifically I would add three category-native ones I saw on the losing sites: SVG wave dividers between sections, a full-bleed hero video of generic drone coastline, and a filter sidebar presented before the visitor has been given any reason to care about the collection.

findings.title: The Wiseman dataset already supports a real archive index — but it is missing the one field that makes the archive read as 45 years old
findings.detail: corporate/data/wiseman.json holds 72 properties with fields: name, short, slug, street, address, zip, area, neighborhood, lat, lng, beds/bedsMin/bedsMax, baths, sqft/sqftMin/sqftMax, price/priceMin/priceMax, phone, url, image, thumb, category. Geography is clean and already hierarchical: area gives West Los Angeles 27, Beverly Grove 14, Brentwood 13, Hollywood 13, Venice 2, Culver City 2, Glendale 1; neighborhood refines to West LA · Sawtelle 26, Brentwood 13, Beverly Grove 11, Fairfax · Sunset 6, Hollywood 5, Venice 2, Culver City · Motor Avenue 2, Pico–Robertson 2, and singletons in Glendale, Rancho Park, Miracle Mile, West Hollywood. 70 of 72 have images; 67 of 72 have price data; 59 of 72 have sqft. The buildings are already named after their streets — Brockton Manor, Beloit at Ohio, Armacost Manor, Amherst Rochester, Penmar Superba, McClellan Corner, West Idaho — which is a gift: the collection is literally a street atlas. What is absent is any temporal field. There is no year built, year acquired, or acquisition sequence. Every index pattern that reads as heritage rather than inventory (HDM's number, Chipperfield's '2022–', OMA's year headings, 6a's Sort by Year, Rudin's '1925 Founded') depends on a date. Without one, a Wiseman index can only be sorted by rent or bedroom count, which is a listings site by definition.

summary:
The Motor Tides repo at `/Users/wangzhen/Documents/wiseman website` is a vanilla HTML/CSS/JS concept set — no framework, no build step, no package manager — comprising 29 pages across 11 concept directories plus a shared 778-line chat widget and a 144-line Python deploy script. For a Wiseman Residential corporate site, three things are directly liftable: (a) the **monogram mask mechanic** (`option-monogram/index.html:76-88, 344-399`), which is ~25 lines of CSS and ~35 lines of JS and is fully portable — the word "WISEMAN" or "45 YEARS" substitutes for "MOTOR/TIDES" with no math changes; (b) **option-e's shared infrastructure** (`option-e/style.css` 579 lines, `option-e/app.js` 438 lines), which is the only concept with externalized CSS/JS and is already structured as a design system — Lenis setup, reveal observers, smart header, page-transition curtain, fullscreen menu, and a six-palette token system that swaps `[data-theme]` on `:root` without touching structure; (c) the **chat widget** (`assets/chat.js`), which is themed entirely through ten `--mtc-*` custom properties and has a clean flow/router separation that re-scripts for a portfolio in roughly a day.

The most valuable inheritance, though, is the trap list. The git history (`git log` on 12 commits) is unusually rich: each commit message documents a measured failure — descenders clipped by 0.098em masks, buttons clipped 59px by `flex:1` + `min-width`, a lockup that zoomed *backward* and undid its own reveal, gold display type that failed contrast on bright photography. Combined with the inline comments, this yields about a dozen hard rules a new site should inherit rather than rediscover: `overflow-x:clip` never `hidden` (sticky dies under `hidden`), `padding-top`/`padding-bottom` longhand on any element that is also `.wrap` (shorthand kills the `var(--pad)` gutter), `svh` alongside `vh` for every pinned stage, reduced-motion collapses that still paint the static image, and cache-bust query params that must be hand-bumped. Note also that `/Users/wangzhen/Documents/wiseman website/corporate/data/properties.psv` already exists — 72 properties with name, category, beds, baths, sqft, address, price, phone, RentCafe path, and image path — so the corporate site's data layer is scaffolded and its images sit on the same RentCafe CDN the deploy rewrites already target.
recommendations: Start the corporate site from option-e, not from a blank page or from monogram. It is the only concept with externalized `style.css` + `app.js`, and a ~72-property site cannot carry an inlined stylesheet per page. Copy `option-e/style.css` and `option-e/app.js` into a new `corporate/` tree, then delete the concept-specific halves of app.js (hero letter-splitter 131-159, chapter sweep 175-212, sliders 214-245, tours strip 247-265, plan preview 267-296, map 298-322, experience rail 324-337, theme-switcher UI 60-101) and keep the generic spine (Lenis 7-31, page transitions 34-58, menu 105-129, reveals 161-172, stepper 340-372, per-frame scroll 374-438).

Port the mask mechanic as a standalone component, and port the `--vh100` fix with it. The whole effect is ~25 lines of CSS (option-monogram:76-88) and ~35 lines of JS (344-399). Substitute the two `<span>` children — 'WISEMAN' / 'RESIDENTIAL', or '45' / 'YEARS' — and change nothing else in the phase math. But replace the stage's `height:100vh` and the section's `300vh/340vh` with option-e's `--vh100` token plus an `@supports (height:100svh)` override; monogram's omission of that is its one unfixed mobile flaw.

Keep the mask's forward-only invariant as a hard rule. Commit f27d2fe established it by measurement: scale must never decrease on either the lockup or the full frame, verified over a 41-point sweep. If a new chapter wants a second mask moment, give it a different photograph and a larger peak — do not contract the first one back down. Re-run a sweep (sample p at 41 points, assert monotonic non-decreasing scale) after any timing change.

Use the corporate site's mask for the ONE identity moment, not per-property. With 72 properties, a scroll-scrubbed 7.2x clipped-text bloom on every property page would be both a performance problem and a cliché by the third page. One hero-scale mask on the corporate home — the surf or an LA skyline inside the Wiseman wordmark — then let property pages use the quieter option-e curtain/reveal vocabulary.

Build the property index off `corporate/data/properties.psv` (72 rows, `name|category|beds|baths|sqft|address|price|phone|path|image`) and reuse the hub's card grid at `redesign/index.html:86-110` as the starting layout — `grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fit,minmax(250px,1fr))` with a `.card.featured{grid-column:1/-1;flex-direction:row}` variant for spotlighting. The `category` column already partitions the portfolio (23 West LA, 23 Hollywood, 18 unlabeled, 6 Brentwood, 1 Culver City, 1 Condo/West LA) and is the natural filter axis.

Extend prep_deploy.py rather than replacing it, but fix three things: make `ROOT` repo-relative instead of the hardcoded absolute path at line 11; generalize `MAP` from a hand-written dict to a read of `properties.psv` (its `image` column already holds `s3/<n>/<id>/<file>` paths, though note they span many s3 buckets while the current `CDN` template hardcodes `s3/2/9707` — the bucket must become part of the mapping); and stamp `?v=` query params from a content hash at build time instead of leaving them hand-maintained. Keep the `(` / `)` percent-encoding at line 73 and keep the post-build sanity grep at 137-142.

Re-script the chat widget as a portfolio concierge by adding conversation state, not by editing copy. Introduce a module-level `selected` property, a `flowFindHome()` that filters the PROPERTIES array by neighborhood/beds/budget and renders results through the existing `.mtc-card` renderer (chat.js:550-554), and a `selectProperty()` setter; then make `flowPricing`, `flowTour`, `flowApply`, `flowLocation`, `flowHours`, `flowParking` read `selected` and ask which community when it is null. Thread the per-property `phone` and RentCafe `path` from the PSV in place of the module constants `APPLY_URL`/`TEL`/`TEL_LABEL` (chat.js:48-50). Add a neighborhood branch to the router ladder ahead of the generic location match. Leave the engine — styles, scaffold, bot()/chips(), variant allowlist, audio arming, reduced-motion guards — untouched.

Adopt the `data-sec="light|dark"` contract on every top-level section from day one. It is what lets the header and stepper adapt to whatever is beneath them with zero per-page configuration (app.js:393-415), and retrofitting it across 70+ pages later is far more work than writing it as you go.

Use `absTop()` (offsetTop/offsetParent walk), never `getBoundingClientRect().top + scrollY`, for any scroll-spy, stepper, or anchor-landing math — because `.rv` reveals apply a 24px transform that corrupts rect measurements before reveal (app.js:344-345 and the comment above it). And carry the deep-link correction at app.js:416-428 verbatim, including the `hashDone` wheel/touch guard; a portfolio site will be deep-linked into heavily and its imagery shifts layout late.

Codify the trap list in a CONVENTIONS.md at the new site's root before writing the second page: `overflow-x:clip` never `hidden`; `padding-top`/`padding-bottom` longhand on any `.wrap` element (shorthand kills the gutter — full-bleed sections get an inner `.wrap` instead); `vh` always paired with an `@supports (height:100svh)` twin; `flex:1 1 auto; min-width:max-content` on flex buttons with nowrap labels; `overflow:hidden` line masks extended `.14em` with a matching negative margin; two-token accents (`--x` decorative, `--x-ink` text-safe) with body copy always on the AA neutral; dark themes require an explicit hover-state sweep, not just a token flip; `.js` class gating so content is visible if scripts fail; `pageshow`+`e.persisted` reset on the transition curtain; modifier-key bail on intercepted links. Each of these cost a debugging session already.

Check the header at 375px on day one. Commit 37e459f found the brand lockup and CTA wrapping to two lines inside a 62px bar on every single concept — it is the repo's most reliable regression. Scope all fixes `max-width`-only so desktop stays untouched.
donots: Do not claim the floor-plan-drawing-to-plan-name mapping is confirmed. Both READMEs and CONTENT.md state it is INFERRED from bedroom and unit-stack counts and has not been verified by Wiseman. Carry that caveat into any client conversation.

Do not restate prices, unit counts, availability, or contact info as authoritative. CONTENT.md's standing rule is 'NEVER invent prices, unit counts, or contact info,' and the live leasing system is the authority. Link out to SecureCafe/RentCafe rather than duplicating. This risk scales by 72 on a corporate site.

Do not give each word its own `background-clip:text` element. That was the original monogram design and it showed a separate copy of the photo per word; the fix (commit f27d2fe) was a single clipping canvas with block-level spans. Reverting to per-word elements reintroduces per-word alignment math and breaks the continuous-image illusion.
Do not let the mask scale ever decrease. A contraction undoes the reveal it just paid off — this is the explicit lesson of commit f27d2fe and the reason the runway was cut from 520vh to 340vh.

Do not use `overflow-x:hidden` on html or body. It creates a scroll container that silently kills `position:sticky`, which every pinned stage, curtain, and mask depends on. There is no error message; the choreography just stops working.

Do not put `background-position` (or any repainting property) in `will-change` on a clipped-text layer, and do not lift the mobile peak-scale cap of 4.8x below 700px — both were deliberate performance fixes.

Do not write shorthand `padding: X 0` on an element that also carries `.wrap`. It zeroes the `var(--pad)` horizontal gutter and the text runs to the viewport edge. Full-bleed background sections use shorthand plus a nested `<div class="wrap">`.

Do not add a breakpoint override to the `.lock` font-size. One clamp must govern every width — the old 820px override made the lockup jump from 61vw to 84vw across the breakpoint (commit f27d2fe). Widen the clamp instead.

Do not treat a dark theme as a token flip alone. `[data-theme="midnight"]` needs ~15 follow-up hover-state rules (style.css:541-568) because every 'fill with --ink, text goes --cream' hover inverts to invisible. Budget for the sweep.

Do not deploy without running `python3 scripts/prep_deploy.py` first — `deploy/` is gitignored generated output (.gitignore:9-10) and will be stale otherwise. And do not assume the Vercel MCP token can create projects; per the project memory it cannot, so new projects must be created via the `vercel` CLI.

Do not ship a shared-asset change without bumping the `?v=` query param on every page that references it. The archived a/b/c deploy pages already demonstrate the drift — they request `chat.js?v=2` while being served the v4 file, so returning visitors keep the stale copy.

Do not copy option-e's page-transition link interception verbatim without adding the modifier-key bail (`e.metaKey||e.ctrlKey||e.shiftKey||e.defaultPrevented`) that the inline concepts have at option-monogram:507 — option-e's version at app.js:46-51 lacks it, so cmd-click is swallowed.

Do not copy the JS-built mobile menu from the inline concepts (option-monogram:465-493) in preference to option-e's (app.js:105-129). The inline version has no `inert` handling and no focus return; option-e's is the accessible one.
Do not carry the theme-switcher swatch control into production. It is explicitly labeled a 'concept-review control' (style.css:538) and exists to demo six palettes to stakeholders, not to ship.

findings.title: The mask mechanic: one element, one background, scroll-scrubbed scale — never a contraction
findings.detail:
The effect is `background-clip:text` on a SINGLE element containing both words, not one element per word. `.lock` (option-monogram/index.html:84-86) sets `background-size:cover; background-position:50% 50%; -webkit-background-clip:text; background-clip:text; -webkit-text-fill-color:transparent; color:transparent`, with `.lock span{display:block}` (line 86) stacking the two words as block children. The inline comment at lines 82-83 states the reason explicitly: because both words share one clipping canvas, the photo is painted once across the whole lockup and clipped to every glyph, so the two lines read as windows onto one continuous seascape — 'no per-word alignment math.' The prior version gave each word its own background and each showed a separate copy of the photo (see commit f27d2fe).

Structure: `<section class="mask combo" data-mask data-img="...">` (line 245) wraps `.stage` > `.mfull` + `.lock` + `.under` (lines 246-250). `.mask{height:300vh}` / `.mask.combo{height:340vh}` (77-78) provide scroll runway; `.mask .stage{position:sticky;top:0;height:100vh;display:grid;place-items:center;overflow:hidden}` (79) pins it; `.mfull{position:absolute;inset:0;background-size:cover;opacity:0;z-index:1}` (80) is the full-bleed payoff layer sitting BEHIND the lockup (`.lock` z-index:2, `.under` z-index:3).

JS (344-349): one image URL from `data-img` is assigned to BOTH `.lock` and `.mfull` — `var comboImg = 'url("' + combo.dataset.img + '")'` — so the letters and the full frame show the identical photograph, which is what makes the bloom read as the letters opening rather than a crossfade to a different image.

Phase math (367-396). Progress: `var r = combo.getBoundingClientRect(); var span = r.height - innerHeight; var p = clamp01(-r.top / span)` — p runs 0→1 across the section's non-pinned runway. Smoothstep helper `sm(q) = q*q*(3-2*q)` (371). Peak scale `var peak = innerWidth < 700 ? 4.8 : 7.2` (373).
  • p < 0.30 — `ls = 0.94 + (p/0.30)*0.08` (0.94→1.02), `lo=1, fo=0, fs=1`, and `lock.style.backgroundPosition = (38 + p*66) + '% 50%'` drifts the surf 38%→57.8% INSIDE the letterforms. Note backgroundPosition is written only in this branch, so it freezes thereafter.
  • 0.30 ≤ p < 0.66 — `q = sm(clamp01((p-0.30)/0.36))`; `ls = 1.02 + q*(peak-1.02)`; `lo = 1 - clamp01((q-0.28)/0.55)`; `fo = clamp01((q-0.18)/0.6)`. The letters open outward while the full frame fades up. The staggered offsets (0.28 vs 0.18) mean the photo starts appearing before the letters start fading, so there is never a gap.
  • p ≥ 0.66 — `ls = peak; lo = 0; fo = 1; fs = 1 + sm(clamp01((p-0.66)/0.34))*0.06`. The full frame keeps pushing forward 1.00→1.06.
Writes (391-396): `lock.style.transform`, `lock.style.opacity`, `full.style.opacity`, `full.style.transform`, and `under.style.opacity = lo*0.75` (the caption fades with the lockup).

The governing invariant, from commit f27d2fe: **scale never decreases on either element**, verified over a 41-point sweep. The earlier design ran MOTOR alone, bloomed it, then contracted TIDES back down from 6.5x — 'a reverse move that undid the reveal it had just paid off.' Runway was cut 520vh → 340vh in the same change.

findings.title: Mask mechanic gotchas visible in the code and in commit f27d2fe
findings.detail:
Six traps are already paid for:

1. **`@supports` fallback is mandatory.** Line 87: `@supports not ((-webkit-background-clip:text) or (background-clip:text)){.lock{color:var(--ink);background:none;-webkit-text-fill-color:currentColor}}`. Without it, a non-supporting browser renders `color:transparent` text on no background — the headline vanishes entirely. Note it must reset all three of color, background, and `-webkit-text-fill-color`.

2. **`will-change` must NOT list `background-position`.** Line 85 promotes only `transform,opacity`. Commit f27d2fe: 'will-change no longer promotes on background-position.' Promoting a repainting property on a clipped-text layer is a rasterization cost with no compositor benefit.

3. **Peak scale is capped on small screens.** `innerWidth < 700 ? 4.8 : 7.2` (line 373), with the comment at 372: 'a 7x clipped-text texture is too much for a mid-range phone to rasterize.' The commit confirms this was the reason.

4. **One clamp must govern every width.** `font-size:clamp(3rem,min(24vw,38vh),22rem)` (line 84) — the `min(24vw,38vh)` term handles landscape phones where 24vw would overflow vertically. Commit f27d2fe: 'the old 820px override made the lockup jump from 61vw to 84vw across the breakpoint.' Do not add a breakpoint override to this rule; widen the clamp instead. Checked 320px–1920px plus landscape phone.

5. **`white-space:nowrap` on `.lock` (line 84)** — a wrapped word would break the single-canvas illusion, since the background box is the element box.

6. **The hero must not compete with the payoff.** Commit f27d2fe: the opening hero already shows a stacked MOTOR/TIDES logotype, so the payoff is separated by SCALE not composition — hero 45.6vw vs payoff 82.9vw, leading .96 vs .88, plus the image fill. If the new site's hero shows the same wordmark, the mask section must be dramatically larger or the reveal reads as a repeat.

One unfixed weakness to correct when porting: `.mask .stage` uses `height:100vh` (line 79) and the section heights use `vh` (77-78), with no `svh` upgrade. option-e does this properly (`--vh100` with `@supports (height:100svh)`, style.css:22,38,112,127). On mobile the URL bar will make the monogram stage jump. Port the option-e `--vh100` pattern into the mask.

findings.title: Mask reduced-motion collapse: the image stays in the letters, the bloom is deleted
findings.detail:
The reduced-motion handling is the model to copy, because it degrades to a still of the effect rather than removing it. Two halves:

CSS (option-monogram/index.html:153-162): `.mask,.mask.combo{height:auto}` kills the runway; `.mask .stage{position:static;height:auto;padding:70px 0;display:block;text-align:center}` unpins; `.mask .lock{opacity:1!important;transform:none!important}` forces the lockup visible; `.mask .mfull{display:none}` deletes the payoff layer entirely; `.mask .under{position:static;margin-top:14px;justify-content:center;gap:26px}` relocates the caption below.

JS (344-351): the background-image assignment to `.lock` and `.mfull` happens BEFORE `if(reduce) return;` at line 351. This ordering is load-bearing — the reduced-motion user still sees the photograph clipped into the letterforms as a static piece of art. Only the scroll scrub is skipped.

The `!important` on lines 158 is belt-and-braces: under `reduce` the JS returns before writing any inline style, but it guards against a mid-session preference change (note `matchMedia(...).matches` is read once at line 302 and never re-observed — a `change` listener is absent across all concepts, and that is a known limitation, not a bug to reproduce blindly).
